Monday night. Mahima worked through the probability sheet and stopped at question six. In the margin went a note: "I don't see why these events are independent. My attempt gives 0.4, which looks wrong." Mahima thought, if I bring my working, they can see where I'm stuck instead of guessing. Three unclear points went on a list, stapled to the attempt.

Wednesday, office hours. Mahima put the pages on the professor's desk. "I tried this and it breaks here." The professor read for a minute and said the trouble was only in how the sample space had been set up. Ten minutes were enough.

Friday. Farida asked how it went. "Better than I feared. They knew exactly where to look."

qa.a: Mahima stapled the attempt to the list of three unclear points.

qa.q: What was Mahima thinking while writing the margin note on Monday night?
qa.a: Mahima reasoned that bringing the working would let the professor see where the confusion was, so no one would need to guess.

qa.a: Mahima could send the list and the attempt by email first, because the professor could read them before replying.

Thomas, you're going to see Professor Dasgupta tomorrow and your plan is to say 'I don't get thermodynamics'? Sit down. Let me, Rafiq, your old lab senior, tell you what my own professor taught me in second year.
I went to him with exactly that sentence. He sighed and asked, 'Which part?' I couldn't say. We wasted twenty minutes, and I left more confused.
The next week I did it differently. The night before, I tried the three problems I was stuck on and wrote where each one went wrong. Problem two: I didn't know why the sign of work flips. Problem three: I didn't know which formula applies when volume stays fixed. I took my notebook with my attempts in it.
He looked at problem two for ten seconds, tapped one line and said, 'Here. You've mixed up work done by the gas and on the gas.' Five minutes. Solved.
So tonight, try the problems. Mark where you get stuck.

qa.q: What did Rafiq not understand in problem two?
qa.a: Why the sign of work flips.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel after the first twenty-minute meeting?
qa.a: Rafiq felt more confused and probably embarrassed, having used the professor's time without being able to say which part was unclear.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the second meeting work?
qa.a: Trying the problems the night before, noting exactly where each went wrong, and bringing the attempts to show.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt in each of the two meetings?
qa.a: In the first he was likely frustrated, sighing at a question he couldn't answer; in the second he could help in seconds, which satisfied both.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how trying problems first and noting exactly where they broke let a professor find the confusion in minutes.

Professor Bhatt had exactly ten minutes between her 11 o'clock and 12 o'clock classes, and Anirban had one shot before Monday's quiz. The night before, sitting on his hostel bed while Siddharth snored across the room, he made himself do the hard part: try every circuit problem again, alone.
Three of five worked. For the other two he wrote down exactly where he got stuck: 'Q4: don't know which way current flows once the second battery is added. Q5: got 2 amps, answer key says 0.5. Checked arithmetic twice.' He clipped his worked pages together.
At 11:52 he caught her at the staff room door. 'Ma'am, I tried these two. I'm stuck on the direction in Q4, and in Q5 I'm off by a factor of four.'
She glanced at Q5, pointed at one line and said, 'Parallel, not series.' Q4 took three minutes with a quick sketch. At 11:59 she was walking to class, and Anirban was grinning.

qa.q: What answer did Anirban get for Q5?
qa.a: 2 amps, while the answer key says 0.5.

qa.q: How was Anirban likely feeling the night before, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: He was probably anxious, with only ten minutes and a quiz on Monday, and turned that into careful preparation of exactly where he was stuck.

qa.q: What else could Anirban do if ten minutes is not enough next time?
qa.a: Ask for a short slot in office hours, bringing the same kind of marked attempts.

qa.q: How did the short meeting feel for Professor Bhatt?
qa.a: Professor Bhatt could help quickly without being late for class, since the problems and stuck points were already clear.

grounding: Shows a student retrying problems, noting the exact point of confusion and bringing worked pages, so a busy professor can pinpoint it in minutes.
